messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 21
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Chef
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 61

He is a 21-year-old African man who works as a chef, and when he speaks about the assault, he does so in a voice that stays flat for long stretches, as though he is describing something that happened to someone else. Before the assault, his life is organized around work. He likes the rhythm of the kitchen, the heat, the sharpness of knives, the way there is always something immediate to do. He is single and not dating anyone seriously, though he says that before all this he expected that would change naturally, “when I had time for it.” He comes to sessions as a man who still looks young but carries himself cautiously, as if he is constantly checking the room for exits.

The assault happens after he finishes a late shift and accepts a ride home from someone he knows through friends. He does not describe the event in graphic detail, but he returns to the same few moments again and again: realizing too late that he is not safe, freezing, trying to make sense of why his body will not move the way he wants it to, and then the long stretch afterward when he feels emptied out and unreal. In the days that follow, he goes back to work because he thinks he has to. He tells himself that if he keeps moving, keeps chopping, stirring, plating, and calling out orders, he will not have to think about what happened. At first, the kitchen feels like the only place with a clear structure. He can measure, season, taste, repeat. He can be useful.

But the body remembers even when he tries not to. A hand on his shoulder startles him so badly that he nearly drops a tray. The sound of a pan hitting the floor makes his chest tighten. He begins sleeping poorly, waking in the dark with his heart racing, not always from nightmares but from a sense that something is wrong and he cannot locate it quickly enough. Some nights he stays awake until dawn scrolling on his phone without really seeing anything, just to avoid the images that come when he closes his eyes. When the memories come, they do not arrive in a neat sequence; they hit him in fragments—a smell, a voice, the feeling of being trapped—and he feels as though the room around him narrows.

He becomes more guarded with people at work. He used to joke in the kitchen, exchange quick stories during slow moments, and lean in close when the team is crowded around a prep table. Now he keeps to the edges. He notices which coworkers stand too near and which ones ask questions that feel intrusive, even when they are ordinary questions. He is embarrassed by how quickly his body reacts, by how he flinches when someone comes up behind him, and by how angry he becomes at himself afterward. He tells no one what happened. There is a private shame in his silence, mixed with the fear that if he says it aloud it will become more real, or that people will look at him differently because he is a man.

He begins to avoid anything that reminds him of the assault. He stops taking rides from anyone he does not know well. He changes his route home. He declines invitations, especially if alcohol is involved or if he might be expected to stay out late. He notices that his appetite changes, and on some days he eats only because he is at work and food is in front of him. At other times he overchecks everything—doors, locks, the time, the distance between himself and other people. He is often tense in his shoulders and jaw, as if he is bracing for impact. In conversation he pauses before answering, because he is never fully sure what is safe to say.

Over time, he begins to lose confidence in the parts of himself that once felt solid. He says he used to think of himself as someone who could handle pressure, someone dependable in a busy kitchen where mistakes matter. Now he doubts his own reactions. If he gets irritated or jumps at a noise, he feels weak. If he wants to leave a crowded room, he worries he is being childish. Yet underneath his frustration there is grief: for the ease he used to have in his own skin, for the uncomplicated way he once moved through the world, and for the version of himself who assumed bad things happened to other people.

In sessions, he gradually reveals that he still wants to be close to others, but closeness now feels dangerous. He wants to trust again, to go home at night without rehearsing every step, to stand in a kitchen without feeling as though something might happen at any moment. For now, he continues to work, continue to show up, and continue to carry the memory in a way that shapes his days more than he lets on.
